Driven by curiosity, creativity and teamwork, we aim to harness artificial intelligence and NASA's microgravity combustion research to explore smarter fire safety solutions for future space missions.

“Beyond the Stars, Above the Rest.” 🚀
summary:
FlameLab is an interactive website developed by our team, ELIZASTRA, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

Our project explores how gravity, oxygen, airflow, and fuel affect flame behaviour, especially in space.

Users can adjust these variables, observe flame visualizations, compare different conditions, and conduct virtual experiments.

We also provide NASA research references and real-world fire safety examples.

Our goal is to make space combustion science more accessible, interactive, and easier to understand.
details:
FlameLab — Same Fire, Different Gravity

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 | Team ELIZASTRA

1. Project Introduction

FlameLab is an interactive educational platform developed by Team ELIZASTRA for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It explores how combustion behaves under different gravitational and environmental conditions, with particular attention to microgravity and spacecraft fire safety.

On Earth, hot combustion gases rise due to gravity-driven buoyancy, producing the familiar elongated flame shape. In microgravity, this natural convection becomes significantly weaker, allowing flames to develop more spherical shapes under certain conditions. These differences affect heat transfer, oxygen delivery, and combustion behaviour, making fire management in space a unique scientific challenge.

FlameLab was created to make these concepts easier to understand through interactive visualizations, structured virtual experiments, scientific references, and real-world applications. The platform encourages users to investigate combustion scientifically rather than simply memorize theoretical explanations.

Our central message is simple: The same fire can behave differently when its environment changes.

2. Homepage and User Experience

The homepage introduces FlameLab's purpose through its slogan, "Same Fire, Different Gravity." It provides an overview of combustion science and guides visitors toward the platform's main activities.

Its layout is designed to accommodate different levels of scientific knowledge. Beginners can start by exploring basic flame behaviour, while more experienced users can examine experimental variables and supporting research.

The navigation connects three learning stages: exploring combustion visually, investigating its behaviour systematically, and understanding its scientific and practical significance.

This structure creates a learning journey that moves from curiosity toward evidence-based understanding.

3. Interactive Combustion Simulator

The Combustion Simulator is the primary interactive component of FlameLab. It allows users to manipulate five environmental and combustion-related variables:

  • Gravity: Investigates the influence of gravitational conditions on flame shape.
  • Oxygen concentration: Illustrates how oxygen availability can influence flame appearance.
  • Airflow: Demonstrates the effect of moving air on flame direction and distortion.
  • Fuel type: Introduces differences in combustion characteristics associated with different fuels.
  • Fuel supply: Explores how changing fuel availability affects the illustrative flame response.

An animated visualization responds immediately to changes in these settings, helping users connect experimental conditions with observable effects.

The simulator also includes four predefined scenarios: Earth flame, microgravity, airflow effects, and low oxygen. These provide convenient starting points for users unfamiliar with combustion science.

For example, selecting microgravity illustrates why flames may become rounded when buoyancy-driven convection is reduced. Changing airflow then demonstrates how forced gas movement can alter that appearance.

The simulator uses simplified graphical rules for educational purposes. Its outputs are conceptual illustrations rather than precise predictions of real combustion phenomena.

4. Scenario Comparison

FlameLab allows users to save two experimental configurations and examine them side by side.

This feature supports controlled investigations by making it easier to identify which settings have changed between scenarios.

For example, users can maintain identical oxygen, airflow, and fuel conditions while changing gravity. They can then compare the resulting illustrations and consider the scientific reasons behind their differences.

The comparison function reinforces an important experimental principle: reliable investigations require careful control of variables.

Rather than treating each simulation as an isolated activity, users can analyze relationships between environmental conditions and flame behaviour.

5. Virtual Experiment Notebook

The Virtual Experiment Notebook provides a structured environment for documenting investigations.

Users can formulate research questions, name experiments, save configurations, and organize observations. The notebook also supports variable sweeps, allowing multiple settings of one variable to be explored while other conditions remain unchanged.

For instance, a user investigating oxygen concentration can generate a series of virtual runs without repeatedly configuring every experimental setting.

Recorded values can be presented in comparison charts, while CSV export allows further processing in spreadsheet applications.

Importantly, the notebook distinguishes simulated illustrations from measured experimental data. Users can incorporate external measurements while preserving information about their sources, methods, and uncertainties.

This distinction promotes responsible scientific reporting and prevents simplified visual outputs from being mistaken for verified research findings.

6. NASA Research and Scientific Evidence

The research section connects FlameLab's educational content with published scientific investigations.

It introduces combustion studies relevant to microgravity, oxygen availability, flame characteristics, and fire safety. Users can examine the purpose of different investigations, review their findings, and access supporting references.

The evidence library also encourages comparisons between studies by highlighting their experimental conditions and limitations.

This is particularly valuable because combustion behaviour depends on complex interactions among chemical reactions, fluid movement, heat transfer, and environmental factors.

By presenting scientific evidence alongside conceptual learning tools, FlameLab helps users recognize the difference between a simplified model and an experimentally supported conclusion.

The platform therefore encourages critical evaluation rather than unquestioning acceptance of visual results.

7. Historical Space Safety Incidents

FlameLab examines significant incidents from space exploration to demonstrate the consequences of fire-related and oxygen-system hazards.

Apollo 1 (1967) experienced a devastating cabin fire during a ground test, resulting in the deaths of three astronauts. The investigation led to major improvements in spacecraft materials, cabin atmosphere management, and emergency escape procedures.

Apollo 13 (1970) suffered an oxygen tank failure that severely compromised essential spacecraft systems. Although it was not a cabin fire, the incident demonstrated the importance of engineering reliability and emergency preparedness.

Mir Space Station (1997) experienced a fire involving an oxygen-generating canister. The incident produced smoke inside the station and highlighted the difficulties of emergency response in a confined spacecraft environment.

Together, these historical cases show why understanding combustion, oxygen-related hazards, and fire protection remains essential for human spaceflight.

They also demonstrate that scientific research must be translated into practical safety procedures and engineering decisions.

8. Space Technology and Applications on Earth

The website explores how aerospace-related research has contributed to technological improvements beyond space exploration.

One application involves breathing-air equipment used by firefighters. Lightweight systems can reduce physical strain while supporting emergency operations.

Another example concerns fire detection technology. Research involving air sampling and combustion particles has contributed to approaches for distinguishing potential fire hazards from ordinary airborne dust.

Advanced materials associated with aerospace development have also influenced protective clothing and safety equipment.

These examples emphasize the broader value of space research. Technologies developed to address extreme environments can inspire solutions to challenges encountered on Earth.

FlameLab uses these connections to demonstrate that combustion and safety research can benefit both astronauts and terrestrial emergency responders.

9. Research Recommendation Tool

The Research Recommendation Tool helps users identify scientific references relevant to their individual interests.

Users describe their research objectives, select an environment, and provide relevant requirements. The system then evaluates these inputs against a curated collection of sources.

For example, someone investigating fire detection can receive references associated with detection technologies, while a user interested in breathing equipment can explore related technological research.

The tool uses a keyword- and rule-based matching approach to organize recommendations. It does not independently conduct scientific experiments or generate validated engineering designs.

Its value lies in helping users narrow broad research questions into more manageable directions.

This is especially useful for students beginning independent investigations, as identifying appropriate scientific literature is often one of the most challenging stages of research.

10. What Makes FlameLab Unique?

FlameLab's main innovation is not a single feature but the way its components support a connected scientific learning process.

Interactive exploration allows users to investigate combustion concepts through direct manipulation of environmental conditions.

Structured experimentation encourages controlled comparisons, organized observations, and systematic investigation.

Data literacy is supported through experiment records, visualization tools, and exportable datasets.

Scientific credibility is strengthened by linking educational content to research evidence and openly explaining the limitations of simplified simulations.

Research accessibility is improved through personalized reference matching, helping users locate relevant materials without requiring extensive prior experience.

Practical relevance is established through historical spacecraft incidents and examples of aerospace-related safety technologies.

Together, these elements connect four important scientific activities: observation, experimentation, evidence evaluation, and application.

Rather than functioning only as a digital demonstration, FlameLab provides a foundation for developing curiosity and scientific reasoning.

11. Educational Impact and Target Audience

FlameLab is designed for students, teachers, science enthusiasts, and beginning researchers.

In classrooms, educators can use the platform to demonstrate differences between terrestrial and microgravity combustion. Students can investigate individual variables, formulate hypotheses, and compare observations.

The notebook can support lessons on experimental design, controlled variables, data representation, and scientific interpretation.

For independent learners, the research materials provide opportunities to explore complex topics at their own pace.

The website's browser-based format also makes it convenient to access without specialized laboratory equipment.

Although virtual activities cannot replace physical experiments, they provide a useful introduction to scientific concepts that may otherwise be difficult or unsafe to demonstrate in a classroom.

12. Scientific Limitations and Future Potential

FlameLab currently emphasizes conceptual understanding rather than precise numerical modelling.

Its visualizations are not generated using a validated combustion physics engine and should not be used to predict flame temperature, burning rates, extinction conditions, or spacecraft safety outcomes.

Similarly, research recommendations serve as starting points for investigation rather than professional technical advice.

Future development could include integrating real NASA experimental datasets, implementing more advanced physics-based models, and developing additional methods for analyzing recorded results.

Other potential improvements include expanded educational activities, more detailed visualizations, and stronger connections between published research and virtual investigations.

These developments could gradually transform FlameLab into a more sophisticated platform for combustion education and scientific exploration.

13. Conclusion

FlameLab was developed to make the science of combustion beyond Earth easier to explore and understand.

By combining visual learning, structured experimentation, scientific literature, and practical safety applications, the platform provides an accessible introduction to an important area of space research.

Its greatest strength lies in encouraging users to ask questions, investigate changing conditions, examine evidence, and recognize the real-world consequences of scientific discoveries.

As humanity continues exploring space, understanding fire behaviour in unfamiliar environments will remain essential for protecting astronauts and designing safer spacecraft.

Through FlameLab, Team ELIZASTRA hopes to inspire scientific curiosity, promote responsible experimentation, and encourage future generations to explore the challenges of space science.

Same Fire. Different Gravity. A New Perspective on Combustion.
